lessons.title: Jetpack Libraries: Room Relations, Paging, Navigation and Offline-First
lessons.description: Use more Jetpack: Room relations and migrations, Paging 3, Navigation deep links, SplashScreen, CameraX and offline-first caching.

content.text: Jetpack is the set of Google libraries that solve common app problems. You already used ViewModel, Room, DataStore, WorkManager and Navigation. This lesson adds the rest of the ones you will meet at work.
Room relationships
**One-to-many**: a user has many orders. Put a `userId` foreign key in the orders table, and read both with an `@Relation` class.

**One-to-one** is the same with a single object instead of a list. **Many-to-many** needs a *join table* (for example `StudentCourse`) and `@Relation(associateBy = Junction(StudentCourse::class))`. `@Transaction` makes sure several reads or writes happen together, or not at all. Mark `foreignKeys` with `CASCADE` so deleting a parent removes its children.
Migrations
Turn on `exportSchema` and keep the exported JSON in git so you can write migration tests. Never use `fallbackToDestructiveMigration` in a released app unless losing user data is acceptable.
Proto DataStore and database encryption

**Preferences DataStore** stores key-value pairs. **Proto DataStore** stores a typed object defined by a schema, which prevents key typos. Room itself is not encrypted. For sensitive data, either encrypt the fields you store or use an encrypted SQLite build such as SQLCipher, and think hard about whether you need to store the data at all.
Paging 3

Paging loads a long list in pages as the user scrolls. A `PagingSource` loads one page (from the network or Room), a `Pager` turns it into a `Flow<PagingData<T>>`, and Compose shows it with `collectAsLazyPagingItems()`.
Navigation: arguments, deep links, nested graphs

items: Pass an id, not an object: route `detail/{id}` with `navArgument("id") { type = NavType.IntType }`.
Add `deepLinks = listOf(navDeepLink { uriPattern = "myapp://item/{id}" })` to a destination, and an intent filter in the manifest.
Group screens with `navigation(startDestination = "login", route = "auth") { ... }` (nested graph) so you can leave the whole group at once.
For bottom navigation, save and restore state with `launchSingleTop = true; restoreState = true` and `popUpTo(startDestination) { saveState = true }`.

content.text: SplashScreen, App Startup, Activity Result and CameraX

items: **SplashScreen API**: `installSplashScreen()` before `super.onCreate` shows a consistent launch screen on all Android versions.
**App Startup**: initialises libraries in a defined order from one place, so many libraries do not each slow startup.
**Activity Result APIs**: `rememberLauncherForActivityResult` for permissions, picking photos (`PickVisualMedia`) and documents.
**SavedStateHandle**: ViewModel access to navigation arguments and values that survive process death.
**CameraX**: a simple camera API with use cases for preview, image capture and analysis (used in the QR project).

content.text: Offline-first caching

The recipe: the UI observes Room; a `refresh()` function fetches from the network and writes into Room; errors only show a message because old data is still visible. Add a `lastUpdated` time to decide when to refresh. Use WorkManager to sync in the background with a network constraint.

faqs.q: Why use a join table?
faqs.a: A many-to-many relation cannot be stored in one column, so a third table holds pairs of ids, one row for each link.

faqs.q: Why Paging 3?
faqs.a: It loads only what the user is about to see, caches pages and handles loading and error states, so big lists do not use much memory or data.

faqs.q: What does offline-first mean?
faqs.a: The local database is the source of truth. The network only refreshes it, so the app works without a connection.

lessons.title: Networking in Depth: OkHttp, JWT, OAuth, Pagination
lessons.description: Go deeper on Android networking: OkHttp interceptors, JWT and OAuth, token refresh, pagination, uploads, pinning and GraphQL.

content.text: Project 6 made one simple request. Real apps send authenticated requests, handle failures, upload files, page through results and keep data safe in transit. This lesson covers the pieces behind production networking.
HTTP and REST in short

items: **GET** reads, **POST** creates, **PUT** replaces, **PATCH** changes part, **DELETE** removes.
Status codes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 401 not signed in, 403 not allowed, 404 not found, 429 too many requests, 5xx server error.
Always use **HTTPS**. Android blocks plain HTTP by default, which is the right default.
JSON is the usual format. Kotlin serialization (or Gson/Moshi in older apps) converts it to classes. XML is rare and seen in older APIs.

content.text: OkHttp and interceptors

Retrofit sits on **OkHttp**, which does the real work. An **interceptor** sees every request and response, so it is the right place to add a token, log traffic in debug builds, or add a language header.
Only log request bodies in debug builds. Logging tokens or passwords in a release app is a security fault.
Authentication: JWT and OAuth 2.0

After a user logs in with email and password, the server returns a **JWT** (JSON Web Token): a signed string that proves who the user is. It is short-lived (minutes), and usually comes with a longer-lived **refresh token**. Send the access token in the `Authorization: Bearer` header. When the server answers 401, use the refresh token to get a new access token and retry once. In OkHttp this is an `Authenticator`.

**OAuth 2.0** lets a user sign in through another provider (Google, GitHub) without giving your app their password. Mobile apps use the *authorization code flow with PKCE*, opened in a browser tab or with the Credential Manager for Google sign-in, and never embed a client secret. Use a maintained library (AppAuth, Credential Manager) rather than writing the flow yourself.
Errors, connectivity and results

Wrap calls so the UI receives a result, not an exception: catch `IOException` (no network), `HttpException` (a bad status) and parse the server's error body. Check connectivity with `ConnectivityManager` and `registerDefaultNetworkCallback`, but never rely on it alone: a call can still fail, so always handle errors. Retry only safe (idempotent) requests, with a growing delay.
Pagination, upload and download, caching

items: **Pagination**: page numbers (`?page=2`) or cursors (`?after=abc`). Use Paging 3 to drive it.
**Upload**: `MultipartBody.Part` with a `RequestBody` made from the file. Show progress by wrapping the body. For large or background uploads use WorkManager.
**Download**: stream a `ResponseBody` to a file in chunks, never load it all in memory.
**Caching**: OkHttp can cache responses that allow it with `Cache(directory, size)`; Coil caches images; Room caches data you need offline.

content.text: Network security

items: Use HTTPS everywhere and do not disable certificate checks, even in tests.

**Certificate pinning** (`CertificatePinner`) makes the app trust only your server's key. It adds protection against some attacks, but if the certificate changes and you did not plan for it, the app stops working, so pin with backups.
Keep secrets on a server. Do not trust the app to hide an API key.
Use a network security config only if you must allow special rules.

content.text: GraphQL

GraphQL lets the client ask for exactly the fields it needs in one request. On Android the usual library is Apollo Kotlin, which generates Kotlin types from your queries. Choose it when your backend already offers GraphQL. REST with Retrofit remains the most common.

The original request is repeated once with the new token.

faqs.q: What is a JWT?
faqs.a: A signed token the server issues after login. The server can verify it without a database lookup. Treat it like a password: keep it in secure storage and never log it.

faqs.q: Is certificate pinning required?
faqs.a: No. It adds protection but also risk if a certificate changes. Many apps rely on normal HTTPS. High-risk apps such as banking often pin.

faqs.q: Where do I keep an API secret?
faqs.a: On your server. A key inside an app can be extracted, so the app should call your server and the server holds the secret.

options: Code that sees every request or response

options: In plain text in a file

quiz.q: Why paginate an API?
options: To avoid downloading huge lists at once

lessons.title: Firebase for Android: Auth, Firestore, Storage, Push, Analytics
lessons.metaTitle: Firebase for Android: Auth and Firestore
lessons.description: Add Firebase to Android: email and Google sign-in, Firestore, Storage, push messaging, Crashlytics, Remote Config and security rules.

content.text: Firebase is Google's backend for apps. It gives you accounts, a database, file storage, push notifications and monitoring without running your own server. It is a quick way to build real-time apps such as the chat project. Its services and screens change often, so use the current Firebase documentation for setup steps and treat this lesson as the map.
Set up a Firebase project

items: Open the Firebase console and create a project.
Add an Android app with your application ID (the one from `build.gradle.kts`).
Download `google-services.json` and place it in the `app` folder. Add it to `.gitignore` if your repository is public and you are not ready to share the project details.

Add the Google services Gradle plugin and the Firebase BoM, then the libraries you need, for example `firebase-auth`, `firebase-firestore`, `firebase-storage`, `firebase-messaging`, `firebase-analytics`, `firebase-crashlytics`, `firebase-config`.
Sync, run, and check the console for the first connection.

content.text: Authentication

items: **Email and password**: `Firebase.auth.createUserWithEmailAndPassword` and `signInWithEmailAndPassword`. Send a verification email and a password-reset email.
**Google Sign-In**: use the Credential Manager API to get a Google ID token and exchange it with `GoogleAuthProvider.getCredential`.
**Phone number**: sends an SMS code, and needs setup of SHA fingerprints and, in testing, test numbers.
Read the signed-in user with `Firebase.auth.currentUser` or a listener, and sign out with `signOut()`.

content.text: `await()` comes from the kotlinx-coroutines-play-services library and turns a Firebase Task into a suspend call.
Cloud Firestore and Realtime Database

**Firestore** stores *documents* (like JSON objects) in *collections*. It supports queries and live listeners and works offline with a local cache. The **Realtime Database** is an older, simpler JSON tree, good for very small, fast data. For most new apps choose Firestore.
Storage, push messaging and monitoring

items: **Cloud Storage**: upload images and files with `Firebase.storage.reference.child(path).putFile(uri)` and get a download URL.

**Cloud Messaging (FCM)**: the server (or the console) sends a push message to a device token. Your `FirebaseMessagingService` receives data messages; notification messages are shown by the system when the app is in the background. On Android 13 and later the user must allow notifications.
**Analytics**: log events like `purchase` or `sign_up` to see how people use the app.
**Crashlytics**: collects crash reports with stack traces from real devices.
**Remote Config**: change values (a banner text, a feature flag) without a new release.
**Performance Monitoring**: measures startup time and network calls.
**App Distribution**: sends test builds to testers.

content.text: Security rules and App Check

Anyone can read your app's `google-services.json`, so the database is protected only by **security rules**. Write rules that require sign-in and limit each user to their own data. Never leave test-mode rules (open to everyone) on a live project. **App Check** adds a check that requests come from your genuine app.

faqs.q: Firestore or Realtime Database?
faqs.a: Choose Firestore for most apps: better queries and scaling. Realtime Database is simpler and fine for small, very fast data.

faqs.q: Is Firebase free?
faqs.a: There is a free plan with limits, and paid usage beyond them. Check current pricing before you build something that will grow.

faqs.q: Can the app be hacked if config is public?
faqs.a: The config file only identifies your project. Security rules and App Check protect the data, so write them carefully.

lessons.title: Android Security: Keystore, Biometrics, R8 and OWASP Mobile
lessons.description: Secure an Android app: Keystore encryption, biometric login, R8, safe communication and the main OWASP Mobile ideas.

content.text: Security is part of every app that handles accounts, money or personal data. The goal is simple: protect the user's data on the device and on the network, and assume that a determined person can inspect your APK. This lesson lists the practical steps.
Login, passwords and OTP

items: Validate on the device for good feedback (email shape, minimum length), and on the server for real. Never rely only on the app.
Never store a password. Store a short-lived token, and ask for the password again for sensitive actions.
Rate-limit and lock out repeated wrong attempts on the server.
OTP (one-time password) codes should expire quickly and be single-use. Let the user request a new one, but not endlessly.

content.text: Android Keystore and encrypted storage

The **Android Keystore** stores cryptographic keys in protected hardware where available, so your app can use a key but cannot read it out. Create an AES key in the Keystore, encrypt the token with it, and store the encrypted bytes. The older `EncryptedSharedPreferences` does this for you but is deprecated in recent versions of the security library, so check the current guidance; a DataStore plus Keystore encryption (for example through the Tink library) is the modern pattern.
Do not invent your own cryptography. Use well-known libraries and the algorithms above, and keep the key in the Keystore, never in code.
Biometric authentication

The **BiometricPrompt** API shows the system fingerprint or face dialog, so you never handle biometric data yourself. Use it to unlock the app or to approve an action, and ideally tie it to a Keystore key that needs authentication (`setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)`). Always offer a fallback such as device credentials.
R8, obfuscation and tampering

R8 shrinks and renames code in release builds (`isMinifyEnabled = true`). That makes reverse engineering harder, but it is **not** security: assume attackers can read your logic. Root detection and integrity checks (Play Integrity API) can raise the effort for fraud-prone apps, but they can be bypassed, so enforce the important rules on the server.
OWASP Mobile ideas and best practice

items: **Improper credential usage**: no keys or passwords in the app.
**Insecure communication**: HTTPS only, validate certificates.
**Insecure data storage**: sensitive data encrypted, and not in logs, backups or screenshots (`FLAG_SECURE` on sensitive screens).
**Insufficient input validation**: validate everything, including deep link and intent data.
**Insecure authentication**: short-lived tokens, server-side checks.
Keep dependencies updated, request only the permissions you need, and mark components `exported=false` unless they must be public.

lessons.title: Background Work and Device Features: Location, Maps, Sensors, Payments
lessons.description: Learn WorkManager, foreground services and alarms, then location, Google Maps, camera, sensors, Bluetooth and payment basics.

content.text: Phones have many features apps can use: the camera, GPS, sensors, Bluetooth and payments. Many of them need permissions and run into Android's limits on background work. This lesson shows the main tools and the rules that decide which one to use.
Choosing a background tool

items: **Coroutines**: work while the app is open and tied to a screen.

**WorkManager**: deferrable work that must finish even if the app closes or the phone restarts (sync, uploads). Add constraints: network type, charging, battery not low. Use `OneTimeWorkRequest` or `PeriodicWorkRequest` (at least 15 minutes) and set a backoff for retries.
**Foreground service**: work the user knows about, with a notification: music, navigation, active workouts. Declare a foreground service type in the manifest.
**AlarmManager**: time-exact alarms (alarm clocks, calendar reminders). Exact alarms need special permission on recent Android versions.
**JobScheduler**: the system API under WorkManager; use WorkManager instead.

content.text: Android limits background work to protect battery: Doze mode, app standby buckets and background start restrictions. Do not fight them. Design for deferred, retriable work, and test on a real device.
Notifications

Create a **channel** (Android 8+), build the notification with `NotificationCompat.Builder`, and ask for `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` on Android 13+. Add a `PendingIntent` so tapping it opens the right screen.
Location and maps

items: Use the **Fused Location Provider** from Google Play services. Ask for `ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION` and `ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION`; request background location only if truly needed, and explain why.
`getCurrentLocation` for one fix, `requestLocationUpdates` for tracking (stop it when the screen goes away to save battery).
**Maps Compose** shows a Google Map with `GoogleMap { Marker(...) }`. It needs a Maps API key from Google Cloud, kept out of the repository and restricted to your app.
**Geofencing** notifies you when the user enters or leaves an area, using `GeofencingClient`.
Decide with the user in mind: precise location is sensitive. Ask only when needed, and delete what you do not need.

content.text: Camera, media and files

items: **CameraX** for photo, video and analysis. **PickVisualMedia** for the photo picker, which needs no permission.
**Media3** (ExoPlayer) for audio and video playback; **MediaRecorder** for recording audio and video.
**Files**: use app-specific storage for your own files, the Storage Access Framework for documents the user chooses, and MediaStore for shared media. Broad storage access is restricted.
**PDF**: `PdfDocument` creates PDFs from views or canvas; `PdfRenderer` shows pages.

content.text: Sensors and connectivity

items: **SensorManager** with `Sensor.TYPE_ACCELEROMETER` and a `SensorEventListener` (register in `onResume`, unregister in `onPause`, or with DisposableEffect). Use step counter sensors or **Health Connect** for fitness data, with the user's permission.
**Bluetooth Low Energy** needs `BLUETOOTH_SCAN` and `BLUETOOTH_CONNECT` permissions on recent Android versions; scan, connect with GATT and read characteristics.
**NFC** reads tags through `NfcAdapter` and intents.
**Wi-Fi** APIs are limited in recent versions; use `ConnectivityManager` for state.
**Speech**: `SpeechRecognizer` for speech to text and `TextToSpeech` for the reverse. **Contacts** and **Calendar** use content providers and need their own permissions.

content.text: Payments

Never process cards yourself. For digital goods sold in the app, Google Play requires **Play Billing**. For physical goods and services, use a payment provider's SDK (Google Pay with a gateway such as Stripe or Razorpay). The app collects a payment token from the SDK, and **your server** talks to the gateway and confirms the order. The food-delivery and e-commerce projects use a demo flow only.

Snippets in this lesson are short patterns, not full projects. They were not compiled here. Paste them into Android Studio and check the current documentation of each library, because versions and API names change. Services that need accounts or keys (Firebase, Maps, payments, AI) must be set up with your own project and keys.
Your task

items: Schedule a WorkManager job with a network constraint and watch it in the Background Task Inspector.
Show your location on a Maps Compose screen with your own key.
Read the accelerometer and show a live number.
List which permission each feature above needs and when you would ask.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Background work survives closing the app.
Location updates stop when the screen closes.
Payment secrets stay on the server.

steps.say: Work tied to a visible screen uses coroutines.
Work that must finish later, even if the app closes, uses WorkManager.
Work the user is aware of, like music, runs in a foreground service with a notification.
Only truly time-exact tasks such as alarms use AlarmManager.

faqs.q: Why did my background work not run on time?
faqs.a: Doze and battery limits delay work. WorkManager is designed to run it when the system allows. Use a foreground service or an exact alarm only when the feature really needs it.

faqs.q: Do I need a Maps API key?
faqs.a: Yes, Google Maps needs a key from Google Cloud. Restrict it to your app and keep it out of public code.

faqs.q: Can the app store card numbers?
faqs.a: No. Use a payment provider SDK so card data goes to the provider, and let your server confirm payments.

quiz.q: When is WorkManager the right choice?
options: Reliable deferrable work that must still run later

quiz.q: What should a payment flow never do?
options: Store or handle raw card numbers in your app

lessons.title: AI and Machine Learning in Android: Gemini, ML Kit, TFLite
lessons.metaTitle: AI in Android: Gemini, ML Kit, TFLite
lessons.description: Add AI to Android apps: call a model safely through a server, stream replies, use ML Kit and TensorFlow Lite, and use AI responsibly.

content.text: AI features are now common in apps: chatbots, smart replies, text recognition and recommendations. There are two ways to add them. A **cloud model** (Gemini, OpenAI and others) runs on a server and is very capable. An **on-device model** (ML Kit, TensorFlow Lite) runs on the phone, works offline, is fast and keeps data private, but is smaller. Pick based on what the feature needs.
Generative AI: how to call a model safely

A generative AI API takes a prompt (and a conversation history) and returns text. Calls cost money and need an API key, so the **key must never be in the app**. Anyone can extract it from the APK and run up your bill. The safe design is: the app calls **your own server**, which holds the key, checks the user, limits usage and calls the model. Firebase offers an AI service that avoids shipping a key and supports App Check; check its current documentation. For learning, you can put a key in `local.properties` and read it through `BuildConfig`, but remember that this is for testing only and the key is still extractable.
Streaming responses and history

Models can send the answer in pieces, so the user sees words appear as they are generated. On Android you expose this as a Flow: each emitted chunk is appended to the last message. Keep the **conversation history** as a list of messages and send the recent ones with each request, because the model has no memory between calls. Store it in Room if users should see old chats.
ML Kit on device

items: **Text recognition (OCR)**: read printed text from an image.
**Barcode and QR scanning**: used in project 17 with CameraX.
**Face detection**: find faces and landmarks (not identification).
**Language identification and translation**: detect a language and translate offline after a model download.
**Smart reply, image labelling, object detection and entity extraction** are also available.

content.text: TensorFlow Lite and recommendations

**TensorFlow Lite** (now also called LiteRT) runs your own trained model on the phone, for example an image classifier. You add the `.tflite` file to `assets`, resize the input to what the model expects, run it and read the scores. Train the model in Python and convert it. For **recommendations** you can start simple: show items similar to what the user viewed, or popular in the same category, and move to a server-side model when you have data. For **AI-powered search**, send a query to a server that uses embeddings, and show the ranked results.
Responsible AI

items: Tell users when they are talking to an AI, and that answers may be wrong.
Do not send private data to a model unless the user agreed and your privacy policy says so.
Never let the model make a final decision about money or safety without a human check.
Filter and limit input, protect the key on a server, rate-limit each user and watch costs.
Test for unwanted outputs and give users a way to report a bad answer.

faqs.q: Can I put an AI API key in my app?
faqs.a: Not safely. Anyone can extract it and spend your money. Use a server, or a service built to avoid shipping keys, such as Firebase's AI features with App Check, and check its current documentation.

faqs.q: Cloud AI or on-device AI?
faqs.a: Cloud models are more capable and need a connection and a server. On-device models work offline and keep data on the phone but are smaller and limited to specific tasks.

faqs.q: How does the model remember the chat?

lessons.title: Testing, Debugging and Performance in Depth
lessons.metaTitle: Android Testing and Performance in Depth
lessons.description: Go deeper on testing and speed: MockK, fakes, Compose and Espresso tests, LeakCanary, ANRs, Baseline Profiles and app size.

content.text: Lesson 14 gave you the basics. This lesson covers what teams use every day: good test doubles, UI tests, debugging tools and the performance work that makes an app feel fast.
Unit tests with fakes and MockK

A test should check one behaviour. To isolate a class, replace its dependencies with **test doubles**. A *fake* is a simple working version (an in-memory repository). A *mock* records calls and returns answers you set. **MockK** is the Kotlin library for mocks, and **Mockito** is the Java-based alternative. Prefer fakes for repositories, and mocks for things that are hard to fake.
`runTest` from kotlinx-coroutines-test runs suspend code and skips delays. Test Flows with the Turbine library (`flow.test { awaitItem() }`).
UI tests

items: **Compose UI tests**: `createComposeRule()`, `onNodeWithText("Save").performClick()`, `assertIsDisplayed()`. Add `Modifier.testTag("list")` where text is not enough.
**Espresso** tests XML views: `onView(withId(R.id.save)).perform(click())`. It still matters for older apps.
**Integration tests** check several parts together, for example a ViewModel with a real in-memory Room database (`Room.inMemoryDatabaseBuilder`).
**End-to-end tests** run a full user flow on a device or emulator. They are slow, so keep a few for the key paths such as login and purchase.
**Test-driven development**: write a failing test, make it pass, then tidy. It suits business rules such as price calculations.

content.text: Debugging

items: **Logcat**: filter by package and level; use `Log.d(TAG, message)`. Read crash stack traces from the bottom of the "Caused by" chain up to the first line from your package.
**Breakpoints and the debugger**: step through code and inspect values; use conditional breakpoints in loops.
**Layout Inspector**: shows the UI tree and, in Compose, how often each composable recomposes.
**Network Inspector**: see requests and responses.
**App Inspection** also shows the database and background tasks.

content.text: Memory, ANRs and profiling

A **memory leak** happens when something holds a reference to an object that should be freed, such as a static field pointing to an Activity. **LeakCanary** (a debug dependency) detects leaks and prints the chain. An **ANR** (Application Not Responding) appears when the main thread is blocked for too long, usually by disk or network work on the main thread; read the trace in Play Console or `/data/anr` and move the work to a background coroutine. The **Android Profiler** shows CPU, memory, network and energy over time.
Faster startup and smoother UI

items: **Startup**: do the minimum in `Application.onCreate`, initialise libraries lazily or with App Startup, and use the SplashScreen API.
**Baseline Profiles**: a file that tells Android which code to pre-compile, which can improve startup and first scrolls noticeably. Generate it with the Macrobenchmark library.
**Macrobenchmark** measures startup and scrolling of the whole app. **Microbenchmark** measures one function.
**UI**: stable keys, avoid unnecessary recomposition, avoid nested scrolling lists, and load images at display size.
**Battery and network**: batch requests, use caching, avoid wake locks, and prefer WorkManager.
**Size**: enable R8 and resource shrinking, use AAB, compress images (WebP), and remove unused libraries. Check the APK Analyzer.

faqs.q: Fake or mock?
faqs.a: Use a fake when a simple working version is easy to write. Use a mock when you need to check that a call happened or force an error.

faqs.q: What causes an ANR?
faqs.a: Blocking the main thread for several seconds, typically with disk, network or heavy computation. Move that work to a background coroutine.

faqs.q: What is a Baseline Profile?
faqs.a: A list of important code paths that Android compiles ahead of time, so the app starts faster and scrolls more smoothly from the first run.

lessons.title: Git, Gradle, CI/CD and Play Store Release in Depth
lessons.metaTitle: Git, Gradle, CI/CD and Play Release
lessons.description: Learn Git workflows, Gradle Kotlin DSL, flavors, signing, GitHub Actions, Fastlane and the Google Play release process.

content.text: A good developer ships reliably. This lesson covers the tools that make builds repeatable and releases safe: version control, Gradle, automated builds and the full Google Play process.
Git and GitHub

items: `git init`, `add`, `commit`, `status`, `log`, `diff` are the daily commands. Commit small, with messages that say why.
Use **branches**: `git switch -c feature/cart`. Merge or rebase back into `main`.
Open a **pull request** on GitHub so teammates can review, and let automated checks run on it.
Add a `.gitignore` for `build/`, `.gradle/`, `local.properties` and keystores. **Never commit signing keys or API keys.**
Resolve conflicts by reading both sides carefully, then run the tests.

content.text: Gradle with the Kotlin DSL
Gradle builds your project from `build.gradle.kts` files. A **version catalog** (`gradle/libs.versions.toml`) lists library versions in one place, so every module uses the same ones.
Build types, flavors and variants

A **build type** is debug or release. A **product flavor** is a version of the app, such as `free` and `paid`, or `staging` and `production`. Together they make **build variants** like `stagingDebug`. Use them for different base URLs, app names and Firebase projects. Put values in `buildConfigField` and read them from `BuildConfig`.
Signing configurations
Read passwords from environment variables or an untracked `keystore.properties` file, never from the build file itself.
Continuous integration

**CI** builds and tests every push automatically. With **GitHub Actions**, a file in `.github/workflows` describes the job. Store secrets (keystore as base64, passwords) in the repository's encrypted secrets.

name: Android CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with: { distribution: temurin, java-version: 17 }
      - uses: gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v4
      - run: ./gradlew testDebugUnitTest assembleDebug

**Fastlane** automates the release steps: building, signing, uploading to Play Console and publishing release notes. Use CD (continuous delivery) to push each tagged build to internal testing automatically.
Play Console in depth

items: **App signing**: use Play App Signing so Google keeps the app signing key. You upload with an upload key.
**Versioning**: `versionCode` must increase for each upload, `versionName` is shown to users, and the application ID is permanent.

**Store listing and ASO**: a clear title and short description with the words people search, a high-quality icon, 4 to 8 screenshots and a feature graphic. Honest descriptions help conversion and trust.
**Policy forms**: privacy policy URL, data safety, content rating, target audience, ads declaration and permissions declarations.

**Testing tracks**: internal (up to 100 testers, instant), closed (invited groups) and open (anyone). Personal developer accounts created recently may need to run a closed test with a minimum number of testers before production; check the current requirements.
**Staged rollout**: release to 5 or 10 percent, watch crashes and ratings in Android vitals, then increase or halt.
**After release**: reply to reviews, fix crashes first, and follow Play policy updates, since apps that break policy can be removed.

faqs.a: They let one code base build different versions, such as staging and production, with their own app ID, name, base URL and settings.

lessons.title: Enterprise Android: Modules, WebSockets, i18n, Wear, TV, KMP
lessons.description: See large-team practice: multi-module apps, environments, WebSockets, localisation, accessibility, Wear OS, TV and Kotlin Multiplatform.

content.text: Small apps can be one module with a few screens. Companies with large apps and many developers need more structure. This lesson is a tour of those practices, so you can recognise them in a job and know what to study next.
Multi-module and scalable code

items: **Feature modules** (`:feature:cart`) own their screens, ViewModels and tests. **Core modules** (`:core:network`, `:core:database`, `:core:designsystem`) are shared.
Use `internal` and API modules so features expose only a small public surface.
**Convention plugins** in a `build-logic` module share Gradle settings (compile SDK, Compose setup), so a new module takes a few lines.
Run tests per module and cache builds (Gradle build cache) so CI stays fast.
**Feature flags** (Remote Config or your own) let you merge unfinished work safely and turn features on gradually.

content.text: Multiple environments

Use build flavors (lesson 29) for `dev`, `staging` and `production`, each with its own base URL, Firebase project and logging level. Hilt provides the right values. Never let a debug build talk to production data by accident.
Real-time communication
**WebSockets** keep a two-way connection open, ideal for chat, live prices and collaborative apps. OkHttp supports them directly, and you can wrap the messages in a Flow.

Handle reconnection with a growing delay, and fall back to polling or push notifications when the app is in the background. **WebRTC** adds direct audio, video and data between devices (video calls). It needs a signalling server and STUN/TURN servers, and most teams use a managed SDK instead of building it.
Localisation and accessibility

items: Put every user-facing string in `strings.xml`; add translations in `values-hi`, `values-es` and so on. Use plurals for counts and format arguments instead of joining text.
Support right-to-left languages (`start`/`end` instead of `left`/`right`).
Format dates, numbers and currency with the user's locale.
Per-app language settings are available on newer Android versions.
Meet accessibility rules: labels, contrast, 48 dp touch targets, large font scaling, no information shown by colour alone, and full TalkBack support.

content.text: Other form factors

items: **Foldables and tablets**: use window size classes and adaptive layouts (list and detail side by side).
**Wear OS**: Compose for Wear OS, small round screens, short tasks, tiles and complications.
**Android TV**: remote and D-pad focus, large text, Leanback or Compose for TV.
**Android Auto and Automotive**: strict templates for safety; you build media or navigation experiences through approved APIs.

content.text: Kotlin Multiplatform

**Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP)** shares Kotlin code, such as networking, data and business rules, between Android and iOS (and desktop and web), while the UI can stay native or use Compose Multiplatform. It pairs naturally with this course: your ViewModels, repositories and use cases are plain Kotlin. Start by sharing one module, such as the API client, and grow from there.
App security audit

Before major releases, check dependencies for known vulnerabilities, review exported components, permissions, logging and stored data against the security lesson, and run a static analysis tool such as Android Lint and detekt.

faqs.q: When do I need multiple modules?
faqs.a: When builds slow down, teams grow, or you want strict boundaries and reuse. A small app can stay in one module.

faqs.q: WebSocket or polling?
faqs.a: Use a WebSocket for live two-way updates while the app is open. Use polling or push for occasional updates and when the app is in the background.

faqs.q: Does Kotlin Multiplatform replace Android development?
faqs.a: No. It shares non-UI code between platforms. You still build and ship each platform's app.

lessons.description: Build a calculator in Kotlin and Compose with its own expression parser, correct order of operations, error handling, a keypad grid and unit tests.

content.text: A calculator looks like the easiest app there is, and that is why it makes a good first project of the next group. The screen is simple, but the logic is real: you must turn the text "2+3*4" into the answer 14, not 20. Many beginners reach for a library or a script engine. Here you write a tiny parser yourself, so you learn how text becomes a result, and you keep all of it in a plain Kotlin object that you can test without a phone.

The screen is a grid of buttons built with `Row` and `weight`, a display that shows the expression, and a line for the result or an error. The state lives in a ViewModel, as in every project you have built so far, so the calculator keeps its value when the phone rotates.
Concepts in this project

items: **Tokenising**: splitting "12+3.5*2" into the pieces 12, +, 3.5, *, 2. A leading minus belongs to the first number.
**Order of operations**: the first pass handles `*` and `/`, the second handles `+` and `-`. This gives the same results as mathematics.
**Failing safely**: the evaluator returns `null` for broken input (a missing number, letters, division by zero) and the screen shows "Invalid expression" instead of crashing.
**Separating logic from UI**: `Calculator` is an `object` with no Android imports. The ViewModel calls it, and unit tests call it directly.
**Grid layout**: `Modifier.weight(1f)` gives each key equal width, and `aspectRatio` keeps keys the same shape.

faqs.a: Running arbitrary text as code is unsafe and heavy. A small parser handles only the characters you allow, so it is safe and easy to test.

faqs.a: Bad input is normal in a calculator. Returning null makes the caller handle it, and the screen shows a message.

lessons.title: Project 12: E-Commerce App with Products, Cart and Checkout
lessons.metaTitle: Project 12: E-Commerce App with Room Cart
lessons.description: Build a shopping app with a product grid from a free API, a Room cart that survives restarts, quantity controls, exact totals in cents and a demo checkout.

content.text: Shopping apps combine nearly everything you have learned: a list from the network, images, a database, state shared between two screens and exact money. This project builds the core of one. The products come from the free Fake Store API, the cart lives in a Room database so it survives closing the app, and the checkout is a **demo** that clears the cart and takes no payment.

A real store needs more: sign-in, addresses, a server that creates orders, a payment provider and legal pages. The lesson shows the correct place for each of these, but it does not pretend that this demo is a finished shop.
Concepts in this project

items: **Network plus database**: products are loaded with Retrofit, and the cart is stored with Room. The cart screen reads the database through a Flow, so it updates by itself.
**Exact money**: prices are converted to cents when a product is added to the cart, and totals are sums of integers. `asMoney()` formats them.
**Upsert**: adding the same product again increases its quantity. `@Upsert` handles both insert and update.
**Derived state**: the total and the cart count come from the lines Flow, so they cannot go out of sync.

lessons.description: Build a real-time chat app with Firebase Authentication and Cloud Firestore, live message updates as a Flow, security rules and push notification handling.

content.text: Chat is the classic real-time app: you send a message and everyone in the room sees it a moment later. Building your own server for this takes time, so this project uses Firebase, Google's backend service. Firebase Authentication handles accounts, Cloud Firestore stores messages and pushes changes to every connected phone, and Cloud Messaging can wake a phone with a notification.

This project needs an account and setup that only you can do: a Firebase project and your own `google-services.json` file. Follow the current setup steps in the Firebase console, because its screens change. The security rules at the end matter as much as the app code, because they decide who can read and write your data.
Concepts in this project

items: **Firebase setup**: create a project, register your application ID, download `google-services.json` into the `app` folder and add the Google services plugin.
**Authentication**: email and password sign-up and sign-in, with the result wrapped in `Result` so the ViewModel can show errors.
**Firestore documents**: each message is a document in `rooms/general/messages` with text, sender id, name and a server timestamp.
**callbackFlow**: wraps a Firestore snapshot listener as a Flow, and removes the listener when nobody collects it.
**Cloud Messaging**: a `FirebaseMessagingService` receives pushes. Sending them needs a server or a Cloud Function.
**Security rules**: only signed-in users can read, a message may only be created with the sender's own id, and nobody can edit or delete.

lessons.title: Project 14: Fitness Tracker with Sensors and a Chart
lessons.description: Build a fitness tracker that counts steps with the step sensor, saves daily totals in Room, draws a weekly Canvas bar chart and asks for permission.

content.text: Phones contain many sensors. This project uses the **step counter**, a low-power sensor that counts steps even when your app is closed. It reports one number: the total steps since the phone last restarted. To show today's steps you must save a starting point for the day and subtract it. That small piece of thinking is the heart of this app.

You will also draw your own chart with a `Canvas`. Charts are common in fitness, finance and health apps, and a bar chart needs only a few lines of drawing code. For serious health data across apps, Google offers Health Connect, which you can study next.
Concepts in this project

items: **SensorManager and SensorEventListener**: register to get values, and always unregister. A `callbackFlow` does both for you.
**Runtime permission**: from Android 10 the step counter needs `ACTIVITY_RECOGNITION`, requested with the Activity Result API.
**Baseline**: today's steps = the sensor total minus the total at the start of today. If the phone restarts, the sensor total resets, so the baseline resets too.
**Room by day**: one row per date key like 2026-11-04, updated as steps arrive.
**Canvas drawing**: `drawRect` for bars and `drawLine` for the goal line, scaled by the largest value.
**Graceful absence**: some phones have no step counter. The screen says so instead of failing.

lessons.description: Build a food delivery app with restaurants, menus, a cart, a live order status Flow and Google Maps showing the restaurant, you and a courier marker.

content.text: Food delivery apps are a good test of state management: browse restaurants, build a cart, place an order, then watch the order change over time. This project builds that flow. The restaurants and dishes are sample data in code, the checkout is a demo, and the order tracking is simulated by a Flow that changes status every few seconds.

The map uses **Maps Compose**, which needs your own Google Maps API key. Without a key the rest of the app works and the map area stays blank. In a real product, the courier position comes from your server over a WebSocket, Firestore or push updates, and a payment provider handles money.
Concepts in this project

items: **Sample data object**: `FoodData` holds restaurants and dishes. Replace it with a Retrofit call later without changing the screens.
**Cart as a map**: `Map<Int, Int>` from dish id to quantity. Adding builds a new map, so state updates correctly.
**Order status as an enum**: `Placed`, `Preparing`, `OnTheWay`, `Delivered`, each with a label for the screen.
**A Flow that simulates a server**: `OrderTracker.track()` emits each status with a delay. A real app would listen to a server instead.
**Maps Compose**: `GoogleMap` with `Marker`s and a camera position. The courier marker moves when the status changes.
**Pure helpers**: `courierPosition` and `totalCents` are plain functions with unit tests.

lessons.title: Project 16: Music Player with Media3 and Background Playback
lessons.description: Build a music player with Media3 ExoPlayer and a MediaSessionService, so playback continues in the background with notification controls and a seek bar.

content.text: A music player has one special requirement: the music must keep playing when the user leaves the app. A screen cannot do that, because Android may destroy it. The player must live in a **service**. Google's **Media3** library makes this much easier. It gives you ExoPlayer, a powerful player, and a `MediaSessionService`, which creates the media notification and lock screen controls for you.

The design has two sides. The service owns the player. The screen is a **controller**: it connects to the service, sends commands such as play and next, and shows the state it receives. That separation is why playback survives rotation, closing the screen and even the app being swiped away while music plays.
Concepts in this project

items: **ExoPlayer**: plays audio and video from URLs and files, and handles buffering and formats.
**MediaSessionService**: a foreground service that publishes the player to the system. The notification, Bluetooth buttons and lock screen all talk to it.
**MediaController**: how the screen connects to the session. It is created asynchronously, so the ViewModel waits for the future to finish.
**Playlist**: `setMediaItems` with metadata for title and artist, and `seekToNextMediaItem` and `seekToPreviousMediaItem`.
**Position polling**: the player does not push the playback position every moment, so the ViewModel reads it twice a second for the seek bar.
**Audio focus and noise**: the player settings pause for calls and when headphones are unplugged.

lessons.title: Project 17: QR Code Scanner with CameraX and ML Kit
lessons.description: Build a QR and barcode scanner with CameraX preview, an ImageAnalysis analyzer, ML Kit barcode scanning, camera permission and safe handling of scanned links.

content.text: Scanning a QR code needs three things: a live camera preview, a way to look at each camera frame, and a model that finds codes in it. Android gives you each piece. **CameraX** is a friendly camera library that follows the lifecycle for you. **ML Kit** is Google's on-device machine learning toolkit, and its barcode scanner runs on the phone with no network.

This project also teaches an important habit: treat scanned content as untrusted input. A QR code can contain any text, including a link to a harmful website. The app therefore shows the content and asks before it opens a link, and it classifies the result so the screen can offer the right action.
Concepts in this project

items: **Camera permission**: asked at run time with the Activity Result API. The screen explains why before asking.
**CameraX use cases**: `Preview` shows the camera, `ImageAnalysis` gives you frames. `bindToLifecycle` starts and stops them with the screen.
**Analyzer**: runs on a background thread for each frame. It must close the `ImageProxy` when done, or the camera stops delivering frames.
**ML Kit BarcodeScanning**: takes an `InputImage` and returns the barcodes found, with their raw text.
**AndroidView**: shows a classic `PreviewView` inside Compose.
**Classifying results**: a sealed class (`Link`, `Wifi`, `Text`) and a pure `classify` function that you can unit test.

lessons.description: Build a banking-style app with secure login, a Keystore-encrypted token, biometric unlock, transaction history, transfer validation and screenshot protection.

content.text: Banking and wallet apps show how much care security needs. This project builds the client side of a banking-style app: sign in, keep the token encrypted, unlock with a fingerprint or face, show transactions and send a transfer. It is a **learning project**. It talks to a backend that you must provide, and it should never be used for real money. Real banking software needs a regulated backend, audits and much more.

The key lesson is the split of responsibility. The app is not trusted: anyone can modify it. So it only helps the user and validates early for good feedback, while the **server enforces every rule** again: who the user is, what the balance is and whether a transfer is allowed.
Concepts in this project

items: **Token, not password**: after login the server returns a short-lived token. The app stores only the token, never the password.
**Android Keystore**: an AES key is created inside protected storage. `TokenVault` encrypts the token with it and saves only the encrypted bytes and the random IV.
**BiometricPrompt**: asks for fingerprint, face or device credentials, and only reports success or failure. The app never sees biometric data.
**Interceptor**: `BearerInterceptor` adds the token to each request, so screens never handle it.
**Validation on both sides**: `BankRules.canTransfer` stops obviously wrong transfers early, but the server decides.
**FLAG_SECURE**: hides the screen from screenshots and the recent apps view.

lessons.title: Project 19: AI Chatbot App with Streaming Replies
lessons.description: Build an AI chatbot app with streaming replies, Room history, a stop button, a fake service for testing and a safe design that keeps API keys on a server.

content.text: AI chat is now a normal app feature. The user types a question and the answer appears word by word. Building the screen is mostly about state: a list of stored messages, plus one message that is still being written. Building it safely is about design: the AI key must stay on a server, history must be limited, and the user must be able to stop a long answer.

To let you build and test the whole app without a key or a server, the project uses two classes behind one interface. `FakeAiService` creates a pretend answer slowly, and `ServerAiService` calls your own backend. You start with the fake one, and switch to the real one when your server is ready.
Concepts in this project

items: **Interface with two implementations**: `AiService.reply(history)` returns a `Flow<String>` that emits the growing text.
**Streaming state**: stored messages come from Room. The partial reply lives in a separate `StateFlow`, and is saved only when it is complete (or when the user stops it).
**Cancellation**: the Stop button cancels the coroutine job. The code catches `CancellationException`, saves what was written and rethrows it.
**History window**: `recentHistory` sends only the last messages, because the model has no memory and long requests cost more.
**Server-side key**: the app sends messages to your server. The server adds the secret key, checks the user, limits use and calls the model.
**Honest UI**: a notice tells users that AI answers can be wrong.

lessons.title: Project 20: Video Streaming App with Media3 and HLS
lessons.description: Build a video streaming app with Media3 ExoPlayer and HLS, a PlayerView in Compose, lifecycle-safe playback, buffering and error states and a video list.

content.text: Streaming video is harder than playing a file. Viewers have different networks, so a good service offers the same video at several qualities and lets the player switch between them as the connection changes. This is **adaptive streaming**, and the most common format on Android is **HLS**, recognised by the `.m3u8` address. ExoPlayer from Media3 supports it with one extra library.

The screen part is also interesting. The player is a classic Android view, `PlayerView`, so you place it in Compose with `AndroidView`. The player holds heavy resources, so its lifecycle matters: it must pause when the app goes to the background and be released when the screen goes away. A `DisposableEffect` is the right tool.
Concepts in this project

items: **Adaptive streaming**: the player downloads small pieces of video and chooses a quality for each from your current speed.
**ExoPlayer**: `setMediaItem`, `prepare`, `playWhenReady`. It picks the right media source from the address.
**PlayerView in Compose**: `AndroidView` with a factory that creates the view and attaches the player.
**DisposableEffect**: registers the player listener and a lifecycle observer, and releases both in `onDispose`.
**States**: buffering shows a progress indicator, and an error shows a plain message.
**Video list**: tapping a card changes the selected video, which recreates the player for the new address.

lessons.metaTitle: Project 21: Job Portal App with Filters
lessons.description: Build a job portal client with a job list, search and filter chips, a detail screen, resume upload with file checks and a multipart application request.

content.text: A job portal is a good last project because it joins list screens, filtering, forms, file handling and backend calls. It is also close to this platform's own purpose. The app has two main screens: a searchable, filterable list of jobs, and a detail screen where the user attaches a resume and applies.

The app needs a backend that you provide: `GET /jobs` returns a list and `POST /jobs/{id}/apply` accepts a multipart request with a cover note and a file. Authentication is left out here to keep the lesson focused. A real portal would use the sign-in pattern from projects 13 and 18 and attach the token to every request.
Concepts in this project

items: **Filtering in plain Kotlin**: `List<Job>.filtered(JobFilter)` combines a text search, a remote-only switch and a job type. It is a pure function with unit tests.
**Derived list**: `JobsState.shown` is computed from the full list and the filter, so the list and filters can never disagree.
**Filter chips**: `FilterChip` for remote and job types, toggled on and off.
**Storage Access Framework**: `ActivityResultContracts.OpenDocument` lets the user pick a file without any storage permission.
**File checks before upload**: `resumeProblem` rejects the wrong type, an empty file and a file over 5 MB. The server must check again.
**Multipart upload**: a text part for the cover note and a file part for the resume, sent with Retrofit.

lessons.title: Android Developer Interview Questions and Answers
lessons.description: Android interview questions with short answers on Kotlin, Compose, coroutines, architecture, performance and system design.

content.text: This lesson is a starting bank of questions that come up in Android interviews, with short model answers. It is not the full list of hundreds of questions that exist, so use it as a base: practise saying the answers aloud, and then give an example from your own projects for each one. Interviewers trust specific examples more than definitions.
Kotlin

items: **val vs var vs const val?** `val` is read-only, `var` is reassignable, `const val` is a compile-time constant of a primitive or String at top level or in an object.
**What is null safety?** Types are non-null by default. `String?` allows null; you use `?.`, `?:`, `let` or an explicit check, and avoid `!!`.
**data class vs class?** A data class generates equals, hashCode, toString, copy and componentN from its primary constructor properties.
**What is a sealed class?** A restricted hierarchy known at compile time, so a `when` can be exhaustive. Used for UI state and results.
**Extension functions?** Add functions to a type without inheriting from it. They are resolved statically.
**inline, noinline, crossinline?** `inline` copies the function and lambdas into the caller to avoid allocations; `noinline` opts a lambda out; `crossinline` forbids non-local returns from it.
**lateinit vs lazy?** `lateinit var` is set later and throws if read too early. `lazy` computes a `val` on first use, thread-safe by default.
**object vs companion object?** `object` is a singleton. A companion object holds members tied to a class.
**What are scope functions?** let, run, with, apply and also; they differ in `this` or `it` and in what they return.
**List vs MutableList vs Array?** List is read-only view, MutableList can change, Array is fixed size and maps to a JVM array.

content.text: Android basics

items: **Activity lifecycle?** onCreate, onStart, onResume, onPause, onStop, onDestroy. Rotation recreates the Activity.
**How do you save state across rotation?** ViewModel, rememberSaveable, or SavedStateHandle. For process death, SavedStateHandle or a database.
**Fragment vs Activity?** An Activity is a window; a Fragment is a reusable UI part with its own lifecycle inside it.
**Explicit vs implicit intent?** Explicit names the component; implicit describes an action and lets the system choose.
**Service types?** Started, bound and foreground; use WorkManager for deferrable background work.
**What is a ContentProvider?** A way to share structured data between apps through URIs.
**Context types?** Application context lives with the process; Activity context with the screen. Avoid leaking an Activity context.
**What is an ANR and how do you avoid it?** The main thread was blocked too long. Move disk, network and heavy work to background coroutines.
**What is the manifest for?** Declares components, permissions, app metadata and intent filters.
**How do runtime permissions work?** Dangerous permissions are requested with the Activity Result API; handle denial and explain why you ask.

content.text: Jetpack Compose

items: **What is recomposition?** Compose re-runs composables whose state input changed. They must be fast and free of side effects.
**remember vs rememberSaveable?** remember survives recomposition; rememberSaveable also survives recreation.
**What is state hoisting?** Moving state up and passing value and callbacks down so the composable is stateless.
**LaunchedEffect vs DisposableEffect vs SideEffect?** Run a suspend block keyed to values; register and clean up; publish state to non-Compose code after each composition.
**derivedStateOf?** Computes state from other state and only notifies when the result changes.
**Why use keys in LazyColumn?** Stable identity for items when the list changes, preserving state and animations.
**How do you avoid unnecessary recomposition?** Stable parameters (immutable data classes), keys, reading state late, and checking with the Layout Inspector.
**Modifier order matters, why?** Each modifier wraps the one after it, so `padding` before `background` differs from after.
**Compose vs XML?** Compose is declarative and has less code; XML is imperative and still widespread in older apps.

content.text: Coroutines and Flow

items: **Dispatchers?** Main for UI, IO for disk/network, Default for CPU work.
**launch vs async?** launch returns a Job; async returns a Deferred value for parallel work.
**What is structured concurrency?** Child coroutines are bound to a scope; cancelling the scope cancels them.
**How does cancellation work?** Cooperative; suspending functions check it, long loops should call ensureActive.
**Flow vs LiveData?** Flow is a Kotlin stream with operators and is not tied to Android; LiveData is lifecycle-aware but simple.
**Cold vs hot flows?** A cold Flow starts per collector; StateFlow and SharedFlow are hot and exist without collectors.
**StateFlow vs SharedFlow?** StateFlow always holds a current value and replays it; SharedFlow has no initial value and configurable replay.
**What does stateIn with WhileSubscribed do?** Shares a flow as state and stops upstream work shortly after the last collector leaves.

content.text: Architecture, data and networking

items: **MVVM?** ViewModel holds state and logic; the view observes and sends events. Fits Compose with UDF.
**Clean Architecture?** Presentation, domain and data layers with dependencies pointing to the domain.
**Repository pattern?** One source for data that hides network and database.
**What is dependency injection and why Hilt?** Objects are provided from outside, which improves testing and structure; Hilt generates the wiring.
**Room vs DataStore?** Room for relational data and queries; DataStore for small settings or typed objects.
**How do you make an app offline-first?** Room is the source of truth; the repository refreshes it from the network.
**How does Retrofit work?** An annotated interface becomes an HTTP client; OkHttp does the requests; converters turn JSON into objects.
**How do you handle token refresh?** An OkHttp Authenticator that gets a new token and retries once.
**Pagination?** Paging 3 with a PagingSource and a Pager; handle load states.
**How would you secure stored tokens?** Encrypt with a Keystore key and keep them out of logs and backups.

content.text: Performance, testing and release

items: **How do you find memory leaks?** LeakCanary and the Memory Profiler; look for long-lived references to Activities.
**How do you speed up startup?** Defer initialisation, App Startup, splash screen API and Baseline Profiles.
**What do you test?** Pure functions, ViewModels with fakes, repositories, and key UI flows. Use JUnit, MockK, Turbine and Compose test rules.
**What does R8 do?** Shrinks, optimises and obfuscates; add keep rules for reflection.
**APK vs AAB?** AAB is the upload format; Play creates optimised APKs per device.
**How do you ship safely?** CI, internal testing, staged rollout, and watching Android vitals and crash reports.

content.text: Scenario and system design questions

For design questions, answer in a fixed order: clarify requirements, list screens, draw the layers, choose storage and network strategy, explain state handling, then talk about errors, offline behaviour, security, testing and scaling. Practise with these prompts.

items: Design a chat app: Firestore or WebSocket, local cache with Room, message states (sending, sent, failed), push for background, pagination of history, and read receipts.
Design a news feed with infinite scroll: Paging 3 with a RemoteMediator, Room as source of truth, image caching, and pull to refresh.
Design an e-commerce cart: local cart in Room, server price validation, checkout via your server and a payment SDK, and idempotent order requests.
A screen is janky when scrolling. Walk through measuring, finding recomposition or main-thread work, and fixing.
Users report the app crashes on one phone model. Use Crashlytics or Play vitals, reproduce on an emulator with the same API level, read the trace and add a regression test.
How would you migrate a large XML app to Compose? One screen at a time, ComposeView interop, shared design tokens, and tests around each migrated screen.

content.text: Coding and machine-coding rounds

Machine-coding rounds ask you to build a small app in an hour or two, such as a to-do list, a quiz, a tip calculator or a paginated list from an API. Your projects in this course are exactly that practice. In the round: clarify, sketch the UiState, write a ViewModel and a simple screen, handle empty, loading and error states, then add tests if time allows. Keep the code readable, and say what you would improve with more time. Common coding questions cover strings, arrays, hash maps, two pointers, recursion and basic trees, so practise on a coding site in Kotlin.
These answers are short summaries from standard Android and Kotlin practice. APIs and best practice change, so confirm details in the official documentation before an interview.
Your task

items: Pick ten questions and record yourself answering them in under a minute each.
For each answer, add one example from your own projects.
Rebuild the tip calculator from memory in 45 minutes and note what slowed you down.
Prepare a two-minute description of your best project: problem, architecture, one hard bug, and what you would do next.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can answer the Kotlin and Compose questions without notes.
You have a project story for architecture and for performance.
You follow a fixed order in system design answers.

steps.say: Start by asking what the product must do and for how many users.
Sketch the screens and the layers.
Choose storage and network strategy, and where state lives.
Finish with errors, offline behaviour, security, tests and scaling.

faqs.q: How many questions should I prepare?
faqs.a: Cover each topic area in depth rather than memorising hundreds. Be able to explain why, and to show an example from your own code.

faqs.q: What if I do not know an answer?
faqs.a: Say what you do know, reason aloud from first principles and say how you would look it up. Honesty and clear thinking score better than guessing.

faqs.q: Should I use Compose or XML in a machine-coding round?
faqs.a: Use Compose unless the interviewer asks otherwise, and be ready to explain the XML equivalent.

options: Explain the idea, give an example, mention a trade-off
